newsitem.title: USA: Broker-dealers seen squeezed by munis on-line.
newsitem.headline: Broker-dealers seen squeezed by munis on-line.

text.p: Municipal bond broker dealers will increasingly feel the squeeze as the internet and other electronic trading systems allow buyers and sellers to cut out the middleman, the fixed-income manager for Raymond James & Associates Inc predicted.

"A lot of our customers will be purchasing securities without talking to our brokers," Raymond James Senior Vice President Van Sayler told the Miami Bond Club Wednesday night. "The growth in the use of internet technologies is fantastic."
Direct trading systems have already made major inroads in the stock market through on-line trading and through direct trading systems such as Instinet, Sayler said.

The municipal market has lagged because of logistical problems, namely the sheer volume of issues and issuers. Only 20,000 to 30,000 different stocks are traded, while there are more than 1.3 million CUSIPs in the muni marketplace.
"In a year or two, that issue is going to be gone," Sayler said.

Increasingly sophisticated databases will not only solve the volume problem, but will enable customers to retrieve information that is now only available to broker-dealers, including spreads and the identity of the seller.
By typing in criteria such as the state, maturities and coupon rates they are looking for, buyers will be able to retrieve lists of available bonds and buy them directly from the seller, Sayler said.

The result will be more consolidation within the industry. He predicted the biggest firms would survive, along with "boutique firms" that carve out niche markets, but that "There's going to be fewer in the middle."
Firms that survive will do so by cutting their own transaction costs. In that regard, brokerage firms will follow the trend already seen in commercial banking, Sayler said.
"To talk to a broker, you're going to have to pay a fee the way some banks are charging a fee to talk to a real live teller," he predicted.
